threats.name: Benchmark construction or counterfactual validity drives the result

threats.name: Knowledge conflicts or temporal training contamination drive multi-hop results

threats.name: Retrieval failure, rather than reasoning or editing, explains performance
threats.detail: A system that depends on retrieval may fail because the relevant edited facts were not retrieved, or because retrieval changes across checkpoints.
threats.ruled_out_by: Measure retrieval accuracy and its relationship to downstream performance; for checkpoint comparisons, freeze retrieval and replay identical passages.

threats.name: A correct final answer comes from an incorrect reasoning path or shortcut

threats.name: External benchmark intermediates conflict with model-internal knowledge
threats.detail: A model may be penalized for not using an external intermediate fact that conflicts with its own knowledge, making the result appear to measure reasoning ability.
threats.ruled_out_by: Evaluate model-verifiable intermediates, replace them with model-generated content, or supply the intermediate knowledge in the prompt and compare variants.

threats.name: Generic capability damage, rather than an editing-specific effect, explains the result
threats.detail: Broad model damage can worsen a measured behavior without supporting a specific mechanism of editing.
threats.ruled_out_by: Compare against norm-matched random perturbations and a damage-response sweep; measure capability and perplexity alongside the target behavior.

threats.name: Evaluation pipeline or generation implementation creates pre/post differences
threats.detail: Pipeline drift, caching, padding, or token-indexing errors can produce apparent performance changes unrelated to the editing method.
threats.ruled_out_by: Run a no-edit condition and validate the pipeline against base-model behavior; re-evaluate with an independent generation implementation and correct token indexing where relevant.

threats.name: Sequential degradation is caused by one especially difficult edit, not accumulated edits
threats.detail: A single disabling or difficult edit can resemble cumulative forgetting attributed to a long edit stream.
threats.ruled_out_by: Apply the suspected edit first and measure its effect separately from the accumulated sequence; track prior-edit retention and downstream capability over edit count.

threats.name: Same-subject performance loss reflects general task difficulty rather than subject collisions
threats.detail: A difficult repeated-subject set could lower scores regardless of the proposed key-collision mechanism.
threats.ruled_out_by: Compare with a distinct-subject set preserving relations and objects, and test whether the drop differs across editing methods.

threats.name: A measured association reflects original-fact probabilities rather than new-target perplexity
threats.detail: An association between pre-edit probability and edit outcome would not establish that the difficulty of the new target explains edit failure if original-fact probability shows the same pattern.
threats.ruled_out_by: Measure the corresponding original-fact conditional probabilities and compare their association with editing outcomes.

threats.name: Automatically extracted or generated content, rather than the editing approach, explains a performance gap

threats.name: Temporal pretraining exposure makes a model appear to edit successfully

datasets.name: ReCoE

Uses direct and chain-of-thought prompting. correct_flip is the percentage of predictions that transition from the original answer to the counterfactual answer. No train/dev/test split is specified. Counterfactual facts are decomposed into atomic facts for editing.

baselines.name: Input-augmentation (InputAug)

baselines.name: QLoRA finetuning
baselines.fair_comparison: Evaluated on the same ReCoE reasoning schemes and Tülu base models as the other editing methods, with direct/CoT prompting; finetuned on the new counterfactual facts. Exact hyperparameter matching is not specified.

baselines.name: MEMIT
baselines.fair_comparison: Evaluated on the same ReCoE reasoning schemes and Tülu base models as the other editing methods, with direct/CoT prompting. MEMIT results are reported for 7B and 13B models; it was not implemented for 33B because of GPU memory constraints.

datasets.name: RIPPLEEDITS
datasets.eval_protocol: Evaluated separately on RECENT (2,000 edits), RANDOM (1,000), and POPULAR (1,000) subsets; the benchmark covers 54 relations. For each model-method pair, retain only edits that are successfully applied and test queries the model answered correctly before editing. For each criterion, compute accuracy per example and average across examples. Generate at most 20 tokens; count a query as successful if an alias of the target appears. For queries with multiple gold targets, score targets separately and count a generation correct if it matches at least one.

datasets.name: MQuAKE-cf
datasets.eval_protocol: Evaluated on the fixed 3K-question subset of the full dataset, selected to avoid knowledge conflicts; covers 2-, 3-, and 4-hop questions and instances with up to four edits. Evaluate each instance independently and in batches of k = 1, 100, 1000, or 3000 instances, injecting the batch’s edits together. Each instance has three generated questions; multi-hop accuracy counts it correct if any one is answered correctly. Chains are filtered so GPT-J can recall the single-hop facts, using 8 in-context demonstrations for that filtering.

datasets.name: MQuAKE-t
datasets.eval_protocol: Built from differences between the 2021-04 and 2023-04 Wikidata dumps; each instance has one real-world edit and a 2-, 3-, or 4-hop question chain. Evaluate instances independently and in batches of k = 1, 100, 500, or 1868, injecting the batch’s edits together. Each instance has three generated questions; multi-hop accuracy counts it correct if any one is answered correctly. Chains are filtered so GPT-J can recall the single-hop facts. Vicuna-7B is excluded from this dataset evaluation because its later training may include the updated knowledge.

metrics.name: Reliability
metrics.caveat: Computed as token-level accuracy under teacher forcing, which can overestimate editing performance by exposing gold target information; the paper additionally reports free-running generation without teacher forcing in Appendix O.

metrics.name: Generalization
metrics.caveat: Computed as token-level accuracy under teacher forcing, which can overestimate editing performance by exposing gold target information; the paper additionally reports free-running generation without teacher forcing in Appendix O.

metrics.name: Locality
metrics.caveat: The paper notes that token-level locality metrics may not fully capture broader behavioral preservation; it also reports Capability and free-running generation results, while acknowledging that broader generation-based evaluation remains necessary.

metrics.name: Prompt KL
metrics.detail: Measures next-token distribution drift at prompt-side positions before predicting the target answer; lower values indicate smaller drift from the pre-edit model.

metrics.name: Target KL
metrics.detail: Measures full-vocabulary distribution drift at target-answer positions; lower values indicate smaller drift from the pre-edit model.

metrics.name: Non-target KL
metrics.detail: For rewrite and rephrase contexts, measures KL after excluding the target token and renormalizing the remaining distribution; lower values indicate smaller drift from the pre-edit model.

controls.name: Pre-edit model
controls.detail: The unedited model is reported as a reference condition in the main results, including 100 Locality.
controls.rules_out: Provides a reference for pre-edit predictions and behavior against which preservation can be assessed.

controls.name: KLOD without prefix preservation, retaining non-target preservation
controls.detail: Removes L_prefix while keeping L_nt.
controls.rules_out: Tests the contribution of prefix-distribution preservation; the comparison with full KLOD measures the effect of removing that term in the reported setting.

controls.name: KLOD without prefix preservation, using full-vocabulary KL at target positions
controls.detail: Removes L_prefix and substitutes L_full, which includes the target token, for L_nt.
controls.rules_out: Alongside the no-prefix/non-target-preservation variant, tests the target-excluded non-target KL design against a target-inclusive KL in the reported ablation.

controls.name: KLOD without non-target preservation
controls.detail: Removes L_nt while retaining L_prefix.
controls.rules_out: Tests the contribution of target-position non-target distribution preservation.

controls.name: KLOD without both preservation terms
controls.detail: Removes L_nt and L_prefix but retains the bounded logit-odds target objective.
controls.rules_out: Tests whether bounded target optimization alone accounts for the locality gain.

controls.name: KLOD without all KLOD components
controls.detail: Uses standard cross-entropy and corresponds to LocFT-BF in the ablation.
controls.rules_out: Provides the standard localized fine-tuning comparison without KLOD's bounded objective or distribution-preservation terms.

controls.name: Thresholded cross-entropy
controls.detail: Uses a sequence-level thresholded-CE target objective; its preservation coefficients are selected for Generalization closest to primary KLOD, with the other listed optimization settings held fixed.
controls.rules_out: Tests whether locality gains are explained simply by adding a stopping threshold to cross-entropy rather than by KLOD's position-wise logit-odds objective.

confounds.name: Locality gains arise merely from weakening the edit
confounds.detail: A weaker edit could preserve unrelated predictions and produce better Locality without KLOD's distribution-preservation account being correct.
confounds.ruled_out_by: Reports Reliability and Generalization alongside Locality; compares KLOD with ablations that remove its preservation terms; measures distributional KL drift; and reports ZsRE scaling results where Reliability and Generalization remain comparable to LocFT-BF while Locality is higher.

confounds.name: A stopping threshold alone explains KLOD's advantage
confounds.detail: The improvement could come from stopping target amplification, regardless of KLOD's position-wise logit-odds formulation.
confounds.ruled_out_by: Compares against sequence-level thresholded cross-entropy at a matched-Generalization operating point; KLOD reports Locality 44.75 versus 37.50 for thresholded CE.

confounds.name: The observed results are run-to-run noise
confounds.detail: The main comparison uses a seed-42 run, so its differences could reflect stochastic optimization rather than a stable method effect.
confounds.ruled_out_by: Repeats KLOD, LocFT-BF, and OVERTONE with seeds 1, 42, and 100 while holding the edit set, pretrained model, editable layer, and hyperparameters fixed; reports mean and standard deviation.

confounds.name: Poor FT-M and AlphaEdit results on Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct are anomalous single endpoints rather than cumulative multi-edit degradation
confounds.detail: Their low 3k-edit endpoint results could be an isolated outcome rather than degradation across accumulated edits.
confounds.ruled_out_by: Reports their performance at 500, 1k, and 3k edits in Appendix H; numerical details are not included in the provided text.

confounds.name: Token-level Locality may not represent broader behavioral preservation
confounds.detail: A method could score well on the paper's token-level locality metric while changing broader behavior.
confounds.ruled_out_by: Not ruled out in the provided text; the authors acknowledge this limitation and state that broader generation-based evaluation across datasets and editing settings remains necessary.

baselines.fair_comparison: Compared in sequential editing on the same base LLMs and with 2,000 randomly drawn update samples, 100 per edit.

baselines.name: ROME
baselines.fair_comparison: Compared in sequential editing on the same base LLMs and with 2,000 randomly drawn update samples, 100 per edit.

baselines.name: MEMIT
baselines.fair_comparison: Compared in sequential editing on the same base LLMs and with 2,000 randomly drawn update samples, 100 per edit.

baselines.name: PRUNE
baselines.fair_comparison: Compared in sequential editing on the same base LLMs and with 2,000 randomly drawn update samples, 100 per edit.

baselines.name: RECT
baselines.fair_comparison: Compared in sequential editing on the same base LLMs and with 2,000 randomly drawn update samples, 100 per edit.

metrics.name: Hidden-representation distribution deviation and marginal-distribution differences

controls.name: Pre-edited model
controls.detail: The original, unedited model is reported alongside edited models and used as the reference in general-capability and hidden-representation comparisons.
controls.rules_out: That post-editing capability or representation results are merely properties of the original model; comparison shows whether editing changes them.

controls.name: Baseline editing methods without AlphaEdit projection
controls.detail: MEMIT, PRUNE, and RECT are measured before and after adding AlphaEdit’s projection code; Figure 6 compares original and projection-added versions.
controls.rules_out: That the gains from adding the projection are simply the baseline methods’ unmodified performance.

confounds.name: Editing gains could come with damage to general capabilities rather than selective knowledge editing
confounds.detail: A model might score well on editing evaluations while losing its broader capabilities, so the editing result alone would not establish preservation.
confounds.ruled_out_by: Evaluate post-edited LLaMA3 on SST, MRPC, CoLA, RTE, MMLU, and NLI; report F1 scores across increasing edit counts and compare with the original model.

confounds.name: Apparent knowledge preservation could coexist with overfitting and a shift in hidden representations
confounds.detail: The editing metrics alone would not show whether sequential edits distort internal representations, an alternative account of the claimed preservation and generalization behavior.
confounds.ruled_out_by: Extract representations for 1,000 factual prompts before editing and after 2,000 sequential edits; visualize with t-SNE and quantify scatter-distribution deviation and marginal-distribution differences.

evidence_standards.name: Results reported as mean ± a dispersion value
evidence_standards.detail: Table 1 presents results in mean ± format, but the experimental text does not identify the dispersion statistic or state the number of seeds/runs. No statistical test or significance threshold is specified.

datasets.name: COUNTERFACT
datasets.eval_protocol: Counterfactual edits; unstructured facts are ChatGPT-generated Wikipedia-style paragraphs, checked for alignment with the structured fact and manually filtered. Extracted-triplet edits use ChatGPT-extracted triplets without filtering. Reports editing accuracy for structured, unstructured, and extracted-triplet settings; no split is stated.

datasets.name: MQUAKE-CF
datasets.eval_protocol: Counterfactual edits; unstructured facts are ChatGPT-generated Wikipedia-style paragraphs, checked for alignment with the structured fact and manually filtered. Extracted-triplet edits use ChatGPT-extracted triplets without filtering. Reports editing accuracy and multi-hop accuracy; each sample has three questions and counts as successful if any one is answered correctly. Multi-hop evaluation uses chain-of-thought prompting with in-context demonstrations for FT, LoRA, ROME, and MEMIT. No split is stated.

datasets.name: WIKIUPDATE
datasets.eval_protocol: Built from the September 2023 Wikidata dump. Real-world updates are identified relative to 2021-04-01 using changes in objects and time qualifiers; Wikipedia page summaries are used as unstructured facts, then checked for alignment with the structured facts and manually filtered. Extracted-triplet edits use ChatGPT-extracted triplets without filtering. Reports editing accuracy for structured, unstructured, and extracted-triplet settings; no split is stated.

baselines.name: FT
baselines.fair_comparison: Compared on the same base language models and dataset/edit settings as the other methods where applicable; the default is one edit at a time. For MQUAKE-CF multi-hop questions, uses chain-of-thought prompting with in-context demonstrations.

baselines.name: LoRA
baselines.fair_comparison: Compared on the same base language models and dataset/edit settings as the other methods where applicable; the default is one edit at a time. For MQUAKE-CF multi-hop questions, uses chain-of-thought prompting with in-context demonstrations.

baselines.name: ROME
baselines.fair_comparison: Compared on the same base language models and dataset/edit settings as the other methods where applicable; the default is one edit at a time. It cannot handle unstructured facts directly. For MQUAKE-CF multi-hop questions, uses chain-of-thought prompting with in-context demonstrations.

baselines.name: MEMIT
baselines.fair_comparison: Compared on the same base language models and dataset/edit settings as the other methods where applicable; the default is one edit at a time. It cannot handle unstructured facts directly. For MQUAKE-CF multi-hop questions, uses chain-of-thought prompting with in-context demonstrations.

baselines.name: IKE (single)
baselines.fair_comparison: Compared on the same base language models and dataset/edit settings as the other methods where applicable; uses one edit at a time.

baselines.name: IKE (all)
baselines.fair_comparison: Compared on the same base language models and dataset/edit settings as the other methods where applicable; uses all edits at one time as an additional scalability setting.

baselines.name: MeLLo (single)
baselines.fair_comparison: Compared on the same base language models and dataset/edit settings as the other methods where applicable; uses one edit at a time. Evaluated only with GPT-J and Mistral because GPT2-XL's reasoning ability was considered insufficient.

baselines.name: MeLLo (all)
baselines.fair_comparison: Compared on the same base language models and dataset/edit settings as the other methods where applicable; uses all edits at one time as an additional scalability setting. Evaluated only with GPT-J and Mistral because GPT2-XL's reasoning ability was considered insufficient.

metrics.name: Editing accuracy
metrics.caveat: Measures whether target edits succeed; the authors note that evaluation of performance on paraphrased and irrelevant facts is left for future work.

metrics.name: Multi-hop accuracy
metrics.caveat: For MQUAKE-CF, each sample has three questions and is counted successful if any one is answered correctly; the paper also reports editing accuracy.

metrics.name: Retrieval accuracy
metrics.caveat: Used to diagnose IKE's performance on structured versus unstructured facts; the paper reports it alongside editing results, but does not state a caveat for the metric.

confounds.name: IKE's decline on unstructured facts may come from retrieval failure rather than reasoning failure
confounds.detail: The headline performance drop could reflect failure to retrieve the relevant stored fact, rather than difficulty reasoning from a retrieved fact.
confounds.ruled_out_by: Measures IKE (all) retrieval accuracy on structured and unstructured facts. Accuracy stays close on COUNTERFACT and MQUAKE-CF, while dropping substantially on WIKIUPDATE; the authors infer reasoning is the main issue for the former datasets and both retrieval and reasoning for WIKIUPDATE.

confounds.name: Mistral may perform relatively well on WIKIUPDATE because its training data includes knowledge after the update timestamp
confounds.detail: The model may already know updates dated after 2021-04-01, making its results look stronger without the editing method accounting for the update.
confounds.ruled_out_by: Not ruled out: the authors raise this as a probable explanation but report no measurement to test it.

evidence_standards.name: MQUAKE-CF multi-hop prompting condition
evidence_standards.detail: For FT, LoRA, ROME, and MEMIT, multi-hop results use chain-of-thought prompting with in-context demonstrations. The paper does not report a seed count, variance estimate, confidence interval, or statistical test.

datasets.name: CounterFact
datasets.eval_protocol: Used for the sequential edit stream and primary probe pool. Apply 1,000 sequential edits, evaluating checkpoints at 0, 100, and 1,000 edits. Probes are subject-disjoint from the edit stream and stratified by relation and answer length; 174 of 500 pass the primary Qwen confidence filter. Arbitration is scored as a log-probability contrast across four evidence conditions and three prompt templates. A second split is both subject- and relation-disjoint.

datasets.name: ZsRE
datasets.eval_protocol: Used as a second dataset; 66 probes remain after filtering. The paper reports the arbitration evaluation and ΔAURC against the control; it does not specify a separate edit-stream protocol for this dataset.

datasets.name: MMLU
datasets.eval_protocol: Reported as multiple-choice accuracy for capability evaluation after sequential editing; the paper identifies the questions as four-way multiple choice but does not specify a split.

baselines.name: LoRA-gentle
baselines.fair_comparison: Compared on the same base models and 1,000-edit stream; LoRA applies one edit at a time. The paper says editor regimes are kept natural rather than forced into a shared regime.

baselines.name: LoRA (aggressive)
baselines.fair_comparison: Compared on the same base models and 1,000-edit stream; LoRA applies one edit at a time. The paper says editor regimes are kept natural rather than forced into a shared regime.

baselines.name: MEMIT
baselines.fair_comparison: Compared on the same base models and edit stream, in closed-form batches of 100; upstream hyperparameters are used unchanged. MEMIT and AlphaEdit use the same cached second-moment statistics.

baselines.name: AlphaEdit
baselines.fair_comparison: Compared on the same base models and edit stream; upstream hyperparameters are used unchanged. MEMIT and AlphaEdit use the same cached second-moment statistics.

metrics.name: Mean paired arbitration drift
metrics.caveat: The heavy-tailed distribution lets facts moving in opposite directions cancel, so the mean understates the change; the paper reports the median, dispersion, and AURC alongside it.

metrics.name: Median paired arbitration drift
metrics.caveat: It can vary substantially across seeds; the paper reports AURC and dispersion as more seed-stable summaries.

metrics.name: Arbitration dispersion ratio (sd_after/sd_before)
metrics.caveat: Dispersion alone is not self-evidently harmful; the paper reports AURC to measure whether confidence still orders correct decisions.

metrics.name: Area under the risk-coverage curve (AURC)
metrics.caveat: It is direction-agnostic and does not identify whether the model becomes more credulous or more stubborn; the paper also reports median drift and evaluates end-to-end retrieval. Rescaling margins without changing their ordering leaves AURC unchanged.

metrics.name: MMLU accuracy
metrics.caveat: Unchanged MMLU does not rule out substantial damage to evidence arbitration; the paper measures arbitration directly and compares against a random-perturbation damage-response sweep.

metrics.name: Perplexity
metrics.caveat: The paper notes that perplexity can rise without accounting for the arbitration harm: a perturbation with comparable perplexity produces less harm, while MMLU also falls substantially.

metrics.name: End-to-end retrieval accuracy
metrics.caveat: It measures checkpoint-level performance, not reliably which individual facts will fail; per-fact prediction is reported separately and works for LoRA-gentle but not MEMIT.

metrics.name: Per-fact AUC for predicting retrieval failures
metrics.caveat: It does not reliably predict failures across editors: it improves over pre-edit confidence for LoRA-gentle but not for MEMIT.

metrics.name: Edit success
metrics.caveat: A perfect edit-success score can coexist with capability collapse and arbitration harm; the paper reports MMLU and arbitration measures alongside it.

metrics.name: Neighborhood locality
metrics.caveat: Clean locality does not establish that evidence arbitration is preserved; the paper measures arbitration and capability separately.

metrics.name: Override rate
metrics.caveat: It can suggest increased context trust while obscuring loss of fact-specific discrimination; the paper reports dispersion and AURC.

controls.name: No edit
controls.detail: Run the identical evaluation with no update; it reproduces the baseline to machine precision.
controls.rules_out: That the evaluation pipeline itself manufactures arbitration drift.

controls.name: Norm-matched random perturbation
controls.detail: Apply random low-rank noise in the same layers, matched to the edited arm's realized per-layer update norms.
controls.rules_out: That an equally sized perturbation alone produces the observed arbitration harm.

controls.name: Damage-response sweep
controls.detail: Apply random perturbations at five severities and compare their arbitration effects with their capability damage.
controls.rules_out: That the editing effect is explained by generic capability damage at a comparable or greater damage level.

controls.name: Shuffled targets
controls.detail: Run the same editing procedure with each edit trained toward another fact's target under a seeded derangement.
controls.rules_out: Tests whether the result follows from inserting the intended coherent bindings rather than the editing procedure alone; at 100 edits it reproduces the aggressive LoRA collapse, so that arm is treated as a fine-tuning artifact. The paper says this control is uninformative at 1,000 edits.

controls.name: Temperature-matched base model
controls.detail: Fit a scalar temperature to the unedited model so its confidence matches the edited model's confidence.
controls.rules_out: Whether a confidence-scale difference alone accounts for the result.

controls.name: MEMIT layer ablations
controls.detail: Apply individual saved layer deltas or apply all but one layer's delta to the base model.
controls.rules_out: Whether one layer alone accounts for the effect; the reported results instead show the effect is distributed across the joint update.

controls.name: Frozen retrieval replay
controls.detail: Retrieve the same top-3 passages once with a frozen retriever and replay them for every checkpoint.
controls.rules_out: That checkpoint differences in end-to-end retrieval accuracy are caused by changes in what the retriever returns.

confounds.name: Generic capability damage rather than editing-specific arbitration harm
confounds.detail: A model made broadly worse could show worse arbitration without editing having a specific effect.
confounds.ruled_out_by: Compare with norm-matched random perturbation and a five-severity damage-response sweep using MMLU and perplexity; the sweep produces less arbitration harm even at substantially worse MMLU.

confounds.name: Evaluation-pipeline drift without an edit effect
confounds.detail: The measurement or evaluation pipeline itself could create apparent before/after drift.
confounds.ruled_out_by: The no-edit condition reproduces the baseline to machine precision.

confounds.name: The effect is a target-independent fine-tuning or procedure artifact
confounds.detail: The editing procedure could cause the result even when edits do not install their intended facts.
confounds.ruled_out_by: Use seeded shuffled targets. It reproduces the aggressive LoRA collapse at 100 edits, leading the authors to classify that arm as an artifact; they acknowledge the control is uninformative at 1,000 edits.

confounds.name: Probe facts are affected because they overlap with edited facts
confounds.detail: Apparent arbitration change could concern facts the editor actually touched rather than untouched facts.
confounds.ruled_out_by: Keep probe subjects disjoint from the edit stream and also test a split disjoint in both subject and relation.

confounds.name: The constrained two-candidate probe does not reflect open-ended behavior
confounds.detail: A forced log-probability contrast could change without affecting answers when the model uses real retrieved documents.
confounds.ruled_out_by: Test open-ended end-to-end answers with real retrieval and replay the same retrieved passages across checkpoints; checkpoint-level retrieval accuracy follows the controlled measurement's ordering.

confounds.name: Retrieval quality changes explain the end-to-end result
confounds.detail: An editor's apparent retrieval failure could arise because different passages were retrieved for different checkpoints.
confounds.ruled_out_by: Freeze the retriever and replay the same retrieved passages for every checkpoint.

confounds.name: Confidence rescaling rather than changed confidence ordering
confounds.detail: A scalar change in confidence could affect confidence-based summaries without changing which decisions are more reliable.
confounds.ruled_out_by: Use AURC, which is unchanged by rescaling margins that preserves their ordering, and include a temperature-matched base-model control.

confounds.name: A particular answer string or evidence framing, rather than evidence discrimination, drives the result
confounds.detail: The change could reflect preference for one candidate string or a single passage framing rather than altered discrimination between evidence types.
confounds.ruled_out_by: Evaluate four evidence conditions, including agreeing evidence and three conflicting passages asserting the same alternative with different framing; the paper reports the conditions separately.

evidence_standards.name: Edit-order seeds
evidence_standards.detail: Seeds vary the order of the same 1,000 edits. The paper reports results across three seeds for the relevant runs and explicitly declines to report a Mistral mean because the effect varies substantially across seeds.

evidence_standards.name: 95% cluster-bootstrap intervals
evidence_standards.detail: The paper reports 95% cluster-bootstrap intervals for differences in dispersion ratios; intervals containing zero are treated as not separating the conditions.

evidence_standards.name: Mixed-effects model
evidence_standards.detail: A mixed model uses a random intercept per fact and reports coefficients, standard errors, z statistics, and p-values. Seed is included as a fixed effect because three levels are too few for a stable random-effect variance estimate.

datasets.name: CounterFact
datasets.eval_protocol: Evaluated for Efficacy, Generalization, and Specificity. In the OTE–SE comparison, 2,000 samples are randomly drawn; SE uses 100 samples per step and OTE uses one batch with the same 2,000 samples. The paper does not specify a split or further preprocessing.

datasets.name: ZsRE
datasets.eval_protocol: Evaluated for Efficacy, Generalization, and Specificity; full results are reported. The paper does not specify a split, sample count, scoring details, or preprocessing.

datasets.name: GLUE
datasets.eval_protocol: General-capability evaluation uses SST, MRPC, MMLU, RTE, CoLA, and NLI; performance is tracked as the number of edits increases, and Figure 3 reports F1 scores. The paper does not specify the split, sample count, or preprocessing.

baselines.name: AlphaEdit
baselines.fair_comparison: Compared across the paper’s four base models and reported editing evaluations; the paper calls AlphaEdit OTE-aligned and compares OTE and SE. It does not specify matched hyperparameter tuning.

baselines.name: MEMIT
baselines.fair_comparison: Compared across the paper’s four base models and reported editing evaluations, including OTE and SE; aligned and naive variants are considered. In the OTE–SE comparison, both settings use the same 2,000 CounterFact samples. The paper does not specify matched hyperparameter tuning.

baselines.name: PRUNE
baselines.fair_comparison: Compared across the paper’s four base models and reported editing evaluations; aligned and naive variants are considered, including ablations with and without error correction. The paper does not specify matched hyperparameter tuning.

baselines.name: RECT
baselines.fair_comparison: Compared across the paper’s four base models and reported editing evaluations; aligned and naive variants are considered, including ablations with and without error correction. The paper does not specify matched hyperparameter tuning.

controls.name: Full update rule versus Null-Space Simplified update
controls.detail: The simplified variant drops the terms eliminated using the null-space property; the full version retains them.
controls.rules_out: A difference in language-task performance supports the claim that dropping those terms, rather than merely applying sequential edits, can cause the observed collapse.

controls.name: Pre-edit model
controls.detail: The unedited model’s scores are reported alongside post-edit GLUE scores.
controls.rules_out: Post-edit scores near the pre-edit scores support preservation of general language-task performance relative to the original model.

controls.name: No error correction
controls.detail: PRUNE and RECT are evaluated without the proposed error-correction step, alongside fully aligned versions.
controls.rules_out: A difference tests whether error correction contributes to the aligned methods’ performance, particularly for RECT.

controls.name: Not OTE-aligned (naive) updates
controls.detail: PRUNE and RECT are evaluated without strict OTE alignment, alongside fully aligned sequential versions.
controls.rules_out: A difference tests whether performance depends on OTE alignment rather than simply performing sequential edits.

confounds.name: AlphaEdit’s stability comes from null-space projection itself
confounds.detail: If null-space projection were the key mechanism, applying it in the Memorize-the-Latest task should still yield reliable sequential editing.
confounds.ruled_out_by: The paper evaluates the null-space formulation on CounterFact with LLaMA-3 and reports GLUE scores for the full update versus the null-space-simplified update; the simplified version collapses on the reported language tasks.

confounds.name: The observed failure is due to omitting accumulated terms, not a general benefit of null-space projection
confounds.detail: The paper identifies discarded terms in the update equation as a possible source of accumulated approximation error.
confounds.ruled_out_by: It reintroduces the discarded terms in the full update and reports that this restores language-task performance relative to the null-space-simplified version.

confounds.name: Post-edit hidden-representation shifts are caused by regularization
confounds.detail: The paper considers whether the distribution shift seen after editing is induced by regularization rather than by lack of OTE–SE alignment.
confounds.ruled_out_by: It visualizes pre- and post-edit LLaMA-3 hidden representations for naive and OTE-aligned PRUNE and RECT; the aligned versions show very small shifts.

datasets.name: TOFU factual dataset
datasets.eval_protocol: 217 factual QA pairs about pretrained world knowledge; use 40 forget samples in the main factual setting and use the remaining data for retain and test sets. Rephrased-query evaluation uses queries synthesized by GPT-4. The number of forget samples is varied in a separate experiment; query merging is also evaluated with 80 forget samples.

datasets.name: PISTOL
datasets.eval_protocol: Synthetic knowledge-graph dataset with 400 QA pairs across sales and employment contract types. Finetune the base models on the whole dataset to Rouge1 1.0, then unlearn a portion; the main table uses 20 forget samples, with remaining data used for retain and test sets.

baselines.name: Gradient Difference (GD)
baselines.fair_comparison: Requires a retain set; the paper notes this may be unfair to methods that do not use one.

baselines.name: KL Minimization (KL)
baselines.fair_comparison: Requires a retain set; the paper notes this may be unfair to methods that do not use one.

metrics.name: Rouge1
metrics.caveat: Used as an accuracy proxy based on recall; near-zero Rouge1 on both forget and retain sets can indicate a nonfunctional model rather than successful unlearning. Reported alongside retain-set performance and other metrics.

metrics.name: Mean Reciprocal Rank (MRR)
metrics.caveat: Measures name memorization by averaging reciprocal ranks of target tokens; no further caveat is stated.

metrics.name: Top Hit Ratio (Hit-Rate)
metrics.caveat: Binary check of whether correct tokens fall within the top m output logits; no further caveat is stated.

metrics.name: 1 - Rouge1@Forget + Rouge1@Retain
metrics.caveat: A score close to 1 is ambiguous: it can indicate a non-usable model or a model that did not forget. The paper also reports forget and retain performance separately.

controls.name: Self-improvement pipeline off
controls.detail: Compare WISE and AlphaEdit without the proposed self-improvement pipeline against the pipeline condition.
controls.rules_out: That the reported changes in refusal-answer quality and rephrased generalization occur without the self-improvement pipeline.

controls.name: Query merging off
controls.detail: Compare unmerged ROME and MEMIT with their query-merged conditions.
controls.rules_out: That the reported gains for ROME and MEMIT occur without query merging.

confounds.name: Apparent forgetting is caused by general model failure or damage to retained knowledge
confounds.detail: A method could lower forget-set answer scores by damaging the model more broadly, rather than selectively unlearning the target knowledge.
confounds.ruled_out_by: Evaluate retain-set performance alongside forget-set performance using Rouge1, Probability, MRR, and Hit-Rate; the paper flags near-zero Rouge1 on both sets as nonfunctionality.

confounds.name: A favorable aggregate score masks either no forgetting or a non-usable model
confounds.detail: The combined 1 - Rouge1@Forget + Rouge1@Retain score can be close to 1 in either case.
confounds.ruled_out_by: The paper interprets the score using separate forget- and retain-set results and explicitly notes this ambiguity.

confounds.name: Refusal answers are random, misleading, off-topic, or poorly aligned rather than trustworthy responses
confounds.detail: A model can appear to forget by not giving the target answer while producing low-quality or misleading refusals.
confounds.ruled_out_by: A 20-participant human study rates outputs for trustworthiness and semantic entailment.

confounds.name: Performance on the original queries does not generalize to rephrased queries
confounds.detail: An apparent unlearning result could depend on the evaluated query wording rather than generalizing to paraphrases.
confounds.ruled_out_by: Evaluate on rephrased forget queries synthesized by GPT-4.

evidence_standards.name: Human ratings from 20 participants
evidence_standards.detail: Participants rate trustworthiness and semantic entailment on a 1–5 scale; the paper reports the average. No statistical test, uncertainty interval, or seed-based decision rule is specified.

datasets.name: MQUAKE-CF-3K
datasets.eval_protocol: Counterfactual-edit benchmark with 2-, 3-, and 4-hop questions. Evaluated with edit batches of 1, 100, and all edits. Batches are stratified by question hop count to keep hop proportions relatively similar; edits in a batch are injected simultaneously, except ROME edits them sequentially. Reports multi-hop accuracy and Hop-Acc.

datasets.name: MQUAKE-T
datasets.eval_protocol: Temporal-knowledge-update benchmark with 2-, 3-, and 4-hop questions. Evaluated with edit batches of 1 and all edits. Batches are stratified by question hop count to keep hop proportions relatively similar; edits in a batch are injected simultaneously, except ROME edits them sequentially. Reports multi-hop accuracy and Hop-Acc.

baselines.name: FT
baselines.fair_comparison: Compared on the same benchmarks and edit-batch settings. Parameter-updating methods, including FT, are evaluated on LLaMa-2-7B under both COT and question-decomposition prompting; no further matched tuning protocol is stated.

baselines.name: ROME
baselines.fair_comparison: Compared on the same benchmarks and edit-batch settings. Parameter-updating methods, including ROME, are evaluated on LLaMa-2-7B under both COT and question-decomposition prompting; ROME edits within a batch sequentially because it cannot batch-edit. No further matched tuning protocol is stated.

baselines.name: MEMIT
baselines.fair_comparison: Compared on the same benchmarks and edit-batch settings. Parameter-updating methods, including MEMIT, are evaluated on LLaMa-2-7B under both COT and question-decomposition prompting; no further matched tuning protocol is stated.

baselines.name: MeLLo
baselines.fair_comparison: Compared on the same benchmarks and edit-batch settings. As a memory-based editor, MeLLo is evaluated across all three base language models; the paper reports it with question-decomposition prompting. No further matched tuning protocol is stated.

metrics.name: Multi-hop accuracy (Acc)
metrics.caveat: A correct final answer can result from unreliable reasoning that uses outdated or non-existent facts; the paper also reports Hop-Acc, which checks the reasoning path.

metrics.name: Hop-wise answering accuracy (Hop-Acc)
metrics.caveat: It requires the deduced intermediate-answer path to exactly match the gold path and is available only for sequential question decomposition.

metrics.name: Scope-detector classification accuracy
metrics.caveat: The paper says traditional classification accuracy can lead to underfitting for conflict detection; it instead selects detectors using Success Rate and Block Rate.

controls.name: PokeMQA without the conflict disambiguator (M_dis)
controls.detail: Ablation removes M_dis; the ablation study also evaluates this with M_gen present and absent.
controls.rules_out: Whether performance gains, particularly with larger edit batches, depend on the conflict-disambiguation component rather than the rest of PokeMQA alone.

controls.name: PokeMQA without the knowledge prompt generator (M_gen)
controls.detail: Ablation removes M_gen; the ablation study also evaluates this with M_dis present and absent.
controls.rules_out: Whether performance gains depend on the added knowledge prompt rather than the rest of PokeMQA alone.

confounds.name: High final-answer accuracy may come from unreliable shortcut reasoning rather than correctly following the edited multi-hop path
confounds.detail: A model can reach the right final answer while using outdated or non-existent facts in intermediate reasoning, so final-answer accuracy alone could make its MQA performance look reliable.
confounds.ruled_out_by: Report Hop-Acc, which parses the intermediate-answer path and counts a question as solved only when that path exactly matches the gold path; the paper also analyzes MeLLo reasoning and identifies shortcut patterns.

datasets.name: MMQAKE
datasets.eval_protocol: Evaluation set: 1,278 edits, with 2–5-hop questions (1,278 2-hop, 1,238 3-hop, 1,193 4-hop, and 1,110 5-hop); evaluated using original and visually rephrased images. Questions have paraphrases, and answers are scored as correct when they exactly match an answer in the Wikidata-derived gold alias set. M-Acc scores final-answer correctness; H-Acc requires every intermediate answer in the chain to be correct. The paper does not specify a train/validation/test split for MMQAKE.

baselines.name: Fine-tune (Q-Former)
baselines.fair_comparison: Evaluated with the same three LVLM backbones (BLIP-2, LLaVA-1.5, and MiniGPT-4) and MMQAKE evaluation settings, including original and rephrased images.

baselines.name: Fine-tune (all parameters)
baselines.fair_comparison: Evaluated with the same three LVLM backbones (BLIP-2, LLaVA-1.5, and MiniGPT-4) and MMQAKE evaluation settings, including original and rephrased images.

baselines.name: MEND
baselines.fair_comparison: Evaluated with the same three LVLM backbones and MMQAKE evaluation settings, including original and rephrased images. Parameter-preserving methods such as MEND are trained using the original VLKEB training set of 5,000 editing examples.

baselines.name: SERAC
baselines.fair_comparison: Evaluated with the same three LVLM backbones and MMQAKE evaluation settings, including original and rephrased images. Its counterfactual model is adapted to each LVLM, and parameter-preserving methods are trained using the original VLKEB training set of 5,000 editing examples.

baselines.name: IKE
baselines.fair_comparison: Evaluated with the same three LVLM backbones and MMQAKE evaluation settings, including original and rephrased images; the retrieval-based editing strategy is applied uniformly across models, using the original VLKEB training set of 5,000 editing examples.

baselines.name: LLaMA2-7B (question decomposition)
baselines.fair_comparison: Compared as a decomposition-model alternative with CLIP retrieval and the same LVLM backbones; results are reported on MMQAKE with original and rephrased images.

baselines.name: GPT-3.5-turbo-0125 / ChatGPT (question decomposition)
baselines.fair_comparison: Compared as a decomposition-model alternative with CLIP retrieval and the same LVLM backbones; results are reported on MMQAKE with original and rephrased images.

baselines.name: Gemini 2.5 Flash-Thinking (question decomposition)
baselines.fair_comparison: Compared as a decomposition-model alternative with CLIP retrieval and the same LVLM backbones; results are reported on MMQAKE with original and rephrased images.

baselines.name: MM-Embed (8B)
baselines.fair_comparison: Compared with CLIP as the retrieval model in the module study, with decomposition-model alternatives and LVLM backbones evaluated on MMQAKE.

metrics.name: M-Acc (Multihop Accuracy)
metrics.caveat: Scores only final-answer correctness and may overestimate reasoning ability when the model reaches the correct answer through an incorrect reasoning path; the paper reports H-Acc alongside it and treats H-Acc as the primary metric.

metrics.name: H-Acc (Hop-wise Accuracy)
metrics.caveat: No specific caveat is stated; it requires every intermediate answer in the reasoning chain to be correct, and an instance fails if any step is incorrect.

controls.name: Hybrid-DMKG without Relation-linking Prediction
controls.detail: Ablation removes the linking prediction module while retaining the other components; evaluated across LVLM backbones and original/rephrased images.
controls.rules_out: A gain attributable merely to having the framework components present; the comparison tests the contribution of relation-linking prediction.

controls.name: Hybrid-DMKG without RAG
controls.detail: Ablation uses only the linking prediction module to obtain answers, removing RAG-enhanced LVLM reasoning.
controls.rules_out: A gain attributable merely to having the linking path; the comparison tests the contribution of RAG-enhanced reasoning.

controls.name: Hybrid-DMKG without Background-reflective Decision
controls.detail: Ablation removes the reflective decision module that evaluates competing answers using DMKG background knowledge.
controls.rules_out: A gain attributable merely to producing candidate answers through the two reasoning paths; the comparison tests the contribution of reflective decision-making.

confounds.name: Correct final answers may come from an incorrect reasoning path
confounds.detail: A model can receive credit for a correct final answer despite using outdated or incorrect intermediate facts, making final-answer accuracy look like faithful multihop reasoning.
confounds.ruled_out_by: Report H-Acc, which checks every intermediate answer and counts an instance incorrect if any step is wrong; the paper identifies it as the primary metric.

confounds.name: Answer wording differences may make correct predictions appear wrong
confounds.detail: Exact single-answer matching can penalize semantically valid aliases and understate model performance.
confounds.ruled_out_by: Score against Wikidata-derived answer alias sets; the paper also reports a no-alias evaluation to show the effect of removing alias handling.

datasets.name: zsRE
datasets.eval_protocol: From 19,086 examples, randomly select 2,048; no split-specific sampling is stated. Evaluate with applicable argmax and generate scoring (and, in the generation-length experiment, calculate accuracy at lengths up to 64 tokens). Initial editor comparisons use batch size 16; batch-size experiments use 1, 16, 64, 512, and 2,048 edits. Run on GPT-J (6B) and GPT2-XL (1.5B).

datasets.name: CounterFact
datasets.eval_protocol: From 21,919 examples, randomly select 2,048; no split-specific sampling is stated. Evaluate with argmax, multiple choice (new target sequence succeeds if its likelihood exceeds the original target sequence), and generate scoring; generation-length experiments calculate accuracy up to 64 tokens. Initial editor comparisons use batch size 16; batch-size experiments use 1, 16, 64, 512, and 2,048 edits. Run on GPT-J (6B) and GPT2-XL (1.5B).

datasets.name: MQuAKE
datasets.eval_protocol: From 3,000 examples, randomly select 2,048; no split-specific sampling is stated. Evaluate with applicable argmax and generate scoring (target aliases are checked in generated text); generation-length experiments calculate accuracy up to 64 tokens. Initial editor comparisons use batch size 16; batch-size experiments use 1, 16, 64, 512, and 2,048 edits. Run on GPT-J (6B) and GPT2-XL (1.5B).

datasets.name: RippleEdits
datasets.eval_protocol: From 4,655 viable examples, randomly select 2,048, drawing evenly from each dataset split. Evaluate with applicable argmax and generate scoring (target aliases are checked in generated text); generation-length experiments calculate accuracy up to 64 tokens. Initial editor comparisons use batch size 16; batch-size experiments use 1, 16, 64, 512, and 2,048 edits. Run on GPT-J (6B) and GPT2-XL (1.5B).

datasets.name: LAMBADA
datasets.eval_protocol: Evaluated alongside edits using LM Evaluation Harness; with each edit batch, a chunk of task items is evaluated on the edited model. No split, item count, or task-specific scoring details are stated. Results include accuracy and perplexity.

datasets.name: ANLI
datasets.eval_protocol: Evaluated alongside edits using LM Evaluation Harness; with each edit batch, a chunk of task items is evaluated on the edited model. No split, item count, or task-specific scoring details are stated.

datasets.name: CommonsenseQA
datasets.eval_protocol: Evaluated alongside edits using LM Evaluation Harness; with each edit batch, a chunk of task items is evaluated on the edited model. No split, item count, or task-specific scoring details are stated.

datasets.eval_protocol: Evaluated alongside edits using LM Evaluation Harness; with each edit batch, a chunk of task items is evaluated on the edited model. No split, item count, or task-specific scoring details are stated.

datasets.name: HellaSwag
datasets.eval_protocol: Evaluated alongside edits using LM Evaluation Harness; with each edit batch, a chunk of task items is evaluated on the edited model. No split, item count, or task-specific scoring details are stated. Results include accuracy.

datasets.name: WikiText
datasets.eval_protocol: Evaluated alongside edits using LM Evaluation Harness; with each edit batch, a chunk of task items is evaluated on the edited model. No split, item count, or task-specific scoring details are stated.

baselines.name: MEMIT
baselines.fair_comparison: Compared on the same selected dataset examples, GPT-J and GPT2-XL models, applicable scoring methods, and edit-batch-size conditions as the other editors. The paper uses published MEMIT hyperparameters for these models; no common retuning procedure is stated.

baselines.name: LoRA
baselines.fair_comparison: Compared on the same selected dataset examples, GPT-J and GPT2-XL models, applicable scoring methods, and edit-batch-size conditions as the other editors. LoRA hyperparameters were explored and tuned for batch size 16, so the paper notes this differs from the tuning of the other editors.

baselines.name: in-context editor
baselines.fair_comparison: Compared on the same selected dataset examples, GPT-J and GPT2-XL models, applicable scoring methods, and edit-batch-size conditions as the other editors. No common hyperparameter retuning procedure is stated.

baselines.name: context-retriever editor
baselines.fair_comparison: Compared on the same selected dataset examples, GPT-J and GPT2-XL models, applicable scoring methods, and edit-batch-size conditions as the other editors. The paper says it did not tune context-retriever hyperparameters such as the number of retrieved edits for larger batch sizes.

baselines.name: unedited model (NoEdit)
baselines.fair_comparison: The unedited GPT-J or GPT2-XL model is reported alongside edited models on the same evaluation datasets and general-language tasks.

metrics.name: Argmax accuracy
metrics.caveat: The token-by-token target scoring can yield different editor rankings from multiple-choice or generation scoring; the paper reports results under these alternative scoring methods too.

metrics.name: Multiple-choice accuracy
metrics.caveat: On CounterFact, this scoring method favors MEMIT relative to the other methods; the paper reports argmax and generation results as alternatives.

metrics.name: Generate accuracy (target-alias substring match)
metrics.caveat: Longer generated text increases false positives; substring matches can count an answer as correct when it occurs in unrelated text or for the wrong reason. The paper also reports human assessment and compares alternative generation lengths.

metrics.name: LM Evaluation Harness accuracy and perplexity
metrics.caveat: Most task differences from the unedited baseline are small and show no clear trends; the paper highlights LAMBADA and HellaSwag as tasks that do differentiate editors and batch sizes.

metrics.name: Average number of unique token n-grams (n≤5)
metrics.caveat: Used to investigate whether more varied context-retriever text might explain false positives; greater measured variety does not explain the MQuAKE result.

metrics.name: True-positive, true-negative, false-positive, and false-negative counts/proportions
metrics.caveat: The paper’s exact-match results can include false positives, especially at longer generation lengths; it also manually assesses whether the first answer actually answers the prompt.

metrics.name: Judgment accuracy against human ratings
metrics.caveat: Reported for LLM judges and exact matching on a 200-example human-annotated sample; the paper cautions that the sample is small and calls for further investigation.

controls.name: unedited model (NoEdit)
controls.detail: The original GPT-J or GPT2-XL is evaluated alongside edited models, including on knowledge-editing datasets and LM Evaluation Harness tasks.
controls.rules_out: Provides a reference for distinguishing edited-model scores and side effects from the base model’s unedited performance.

confounds.name: Longer generations create accidental target-string matches rather than genuinely correct answers
confounds.detail: A target alias can appear later in generated text for an unrelated reason, making substring-match accuracy look higher without the model answering the query correctly.
confounds.ruled_out_by: Manually assess 200 examples (150 selected from the late-success class and 50 from the early-success class); raters judge whether the model’s first answer correctly answers the prompt. The paper also reports false-positive and true-positive results by generation length.

confounds.name: The context-retriever’s apparent gain over the in-context editor at longer generation lengths reflects a higher false-positive rate
confounds.detail: More varied generated text could create more opportunities for accidental matches, producing an apparent accuracy gain without more correct answers.
confounds.ruled_out_by: Compare manually assessed false positives across editors and generation lengths, and measure average unique token n-grams. The paper finds a higher false-positive rate for context-retriever in the relevant comparison, while noting that the n-gram result does not explain the MQuAKE case.

confounds.name: A matching substring can occur in an answer that is incorrect or correct for an unrelated reason
confounds.detail: Exact matching may label a response successful even when the first answer is wrong or the matched mention is unrelated to the query.
confounds.ruled_out_by: Human raters judge whether the first answer correctly answers the prompt; the paper compares those judgments with exact matching and also evaluates LLM judges against the human annotations.

confounds.name: Editor rankings may reflect the choice of scoring methodology rather than a consistent difference in editing performance
confounds.detail: The paper observes that editor rankings and absolute scores change across argmax, multiple-choice, and generate evaluation; in particular, CounterFact multiple-choice scoring favors MEMIT.
confounds.ruled_out_by: Evaluate editors using every scoring method applicable to each knowledge-editing dataset and compare the resulting scores and rankings.

evidence_standards.name: Manual assessment of 200 generated examples
evidence_standards.detail: The sample contains 150 late-success examples and 50 early-success examples, drawn equally across datasets within the two classes. Human raters judge whether the first answer correctly answers the prompt; LLM-judge and exact-match accuracy are compared with these ratings. The paper notes the sample is small.

evidence_standards.name: Generation settings used for reported results
evidence_standards.detail: The initial comparison tables use 20 generated tokens. The generation-length analysis generates up to 64 tokens and calculates accuracy at lengths up to 64; the human-rating comparison is reported at 24 tokens. No seeds, confidence intervals, statistical tests, or numerical tie margin are stated.

datasets.name: ScEdit-CF
datasets.eval_protocol: CounterFact-derived counterfactual edits; 1,830 cases, with 7,342 Script-based Efficacy samples and 13,672 Script-based Specificity samples. Human-filtered Script Questions are paired with GPT-4-generated scripts containing the old object; scripts are truncated at the old object’s first mention and concatenated with the question for token-level cloze evaluation. Text-level evaluation uses the Script Questions.

datasets.name: ScEdit-T
datasets.eval_protocol: Uses temporal updates from WDFreal, a WikiFactDiff subset of Wikipedia changes from 4 January 2021 to 27 February 2023; 1,762 cases, with 7,038 Script-based Efficacy samples and 6,597 Specificity samples. Token-level prompts are constructed similarly to ScEdit-CF; specificity examples use nearest-neighbor facts with similar subjects and are scored with S-BO. Llama 3 was not evaluated because its training-data cutoff followed the edited facts.

baselines.name: FT
baselines.fair_comparison: Reported on the same ScEdit tasks and model backbones as the other methods; further matching or hyperparameter-retuning details are not stated.

baselines.name: FT+L
baselines.fair_comparison: Reported on the same ScEdit tasks and model backbones as the other methods; further matching or hyperparameter-retuning details are not stated.

baselines.name: MEND
baselines.fair_comparison: Reported on the same ScEdit tasks and model backbones as the other methods; further matching or hyperparameter-retuning details are not stated.

baselines.name: ROME
baselines.fair_comparison: Reported on the same ScEdit tasks and model backbones as the other methods; further matching or hyperparameter-retuning details are not stated.

baselines.name: MEMIT
baselines.fair_comparison: Reported on the same ScEdit tasks and model backbones as the other methods; further matching or hyperparameter-retuning details are not stated.

baselines.name: PROMPT
baselines.fair_comparison: Reported on the same ScEdit tasks and model backbones as the other methods; further matching or hyperparameter-retuning details are not stated.

baselines.name: Base Model
baselines.fair_comparison: Unedited model results are reported for comparison on the ScEdit tasks; further details are not stated.

metrics.name: ES (Efficacy Success)
metrics.caveat: Assesses preference for the edited over the old object on a basic fact prompt; the paper says fact-based efficacy alone fails to capture editing effectiveness in script scenarios, and reports script-based metrics too.

metrics.name: S-ES (Script-based Efficacy Success)
metrics.caveat: Uses a cloze prompt and compares probabilities of the edited and old objects, rather than evaluating the whole generated script; the paper reports text-level metrics alongside it and finds weak correlation between S-ES and text-level Coherence.

metrics.name: S-NS (Script-based Neighbor Success)
metrics.caveat: Measures retention of the old object for the specified neighbor facts; the paper also reports S-BO for other unrelated neighbor facts.

metrics.name: S-BO (Script-based Bleedover)
metrics.caveat: Measures probability degradation for neighbor facts without the old object; it is a token-level specificity measure, so the paper also reports text-level evaluations.

metrics.name: Exec. (Executability)
metrics.caveat: Does not assess the knowledge update; it measures inherent linguistic/script performance.

metrics.name: Coh. (Coherence)
metrics.caveat: Assesses alignment with the newly updated fact, but the paper finds it weakly correlated with S-ES and reports token-level metrics alongside it.

metrics.name: Cons. (Consistency)
metrics.caveat: Checks stability without mixing old and new facts; the paper reports that it has almost no relationship with token-level metrics, so the measures capture distinct dimensions.

metrics.name: Comp. (Completeness)
metrics.caveat: Does not directly assess the newly edited facts; it probes whether inherent script-related capabilities remain intact after editing.

metrics.name: GE22
metrics.caveat: Uses short bi- and tri-gram entropies, which the paper says cannot fully capture the information in text-level generation; text-level metrics are also analyzed.

metrics.name: Spearman correlation (ρ)
metrics.caveat: The paper treats statistically significant correlations as those with p<0.05 and |ρ|>0.1; it uses the analysis to examine relationships among metrics rather than as a standalone editing-success measure.

controls.name: Base Model
controls.detail: The unedited model is evaluated alongside edited methods.
controls.rules_out: Provides a reference for judging how editing changes efficacy, specificity, and script-related performance relative to the model before editing.

confounds.name: Automatic text evaluation may overestimate or underestimate generated-text quality
confounds.detail: GPT-4 automatic ratings could misstate script quality, affecting conclusions from text-level scores.
confounds.ruled_out_by: Human evaluation of 400 sampled generated scripts by three independent annotators using the same four criteria; the paper reports Krippendorff’s α=0.43 and human–automatic Spearman’s β=0.72.

confounds.name: GPT-4-generated benchmark content may bias ScEdit toward causal language models or include atypical examples
confounds.detail: Benchmark-generated questions and scripts could favor certain model behavior or make results depend on incorrect or atypical samples.
confounds.ruled_out_by: The authors report human filtering of Script Questions and manual checks that partially address incorrect or atypical samples; no quantitative bias test is reported.

confounds.name: MEND’s WikiText-based training may contribute to its performance gap on ScEdit-CF
confounds.detail: The observed gap could partly reflect MEND’s training data rather than difficulty adapting to script-based tasks.
confounds.ruled_out_by: No specific measurement or test is reported; the paper notes this as a possible contributor.

evidence_standards.name: 95% confidence intervals
evidence_standards.detail: Token-level and automatic text-level results are reported with 95% confidence intervals; the paper does not specify the number of seeds or runs.

evidence_standards.name: Human evaluation
evidence_standards.detail: Three independent annotators rated 400 sampled generated scripts on the four text-level criteria; agreement is summarized with Krippendorff’s α=0.43 and human–automatic Spearman’s β=0.72.

evidence_standards.name: Correlation significance rule
evidence_standards.detail: Correlations are treated as statistically significant when p<0.05 and |ρ|>0.1.

datasets.name: SafeEdit
datasets.eval_protocol: The benchmark has 4,050 training, 2,700 validation, and 1,350 test instances. It covers nine unsafe categories; harmful questions are paired with attack prompts to form adversarial queries. Defense Success is evaluated on the test data, while Defense Generalization evaluates harmful questions, attack prompts, or both that differ from the edited instance.

datasets.name: SafeEdit_test_ALL
datasets.eval_protocol: An additional dataset used for the comparison of traditional detoxification methods with knowledge-editing methods. Table 3 reports Defense Generalization on harmful questions alone and on other attack prompts; the paper does not give its size or further split details in the provided text.

datasets.name: TriviaQA
datasets.eval_protocol: Used for Knowledge Question Answering (KQA), measured by success rate with OpenCompass. The paper does not specify the split in the provided text.

datasets.name: XSum
datasets.eval_protocol: Used for Content Summarization (CSum), measured with ROUGE-1 using OpenCompass. The paper does not specify the split in the provided text.

baselines.name: Vanilla (LLaMA2-7B-Chat and Mistral-7B-v0.1)
baselines.fair_comparison: The unedited versions of the two base checkpoints are reported alongside edited models; no further matching procedure is stated.

baselines.name: FT-L
baselines.fair_comparison: Compared on LLaMA2-7B-Chat and Mistral-7B-v0.1. The paper notes that Ext-Sub, unlike the current-instance editing setup, operates on the entire training dataset; it does not specify further matching details for FT-L.

baselines.name: MEND
baselines.fair_comparison: Compared on LLaMA2-7B-Chat and Mistral-7B-v0.1; no additional method-specific fairness procedure is stated.

baselines.name: Ext-Sub
baselines.fair_comparison: Compared on LLaMA2-7B-Chat and Mistral-7B-v0.1. The paper notes that Ext-Sub operates on the entire training dataset rather than the current instance.

baselines.name: SFT
baselines.fair_comparison: For the comparison with knowledge editing, the authors use the additional SafeEdit_test_ALL dataset because traditional detoxification and knowledge-editing methods have different training and testing data settings.

baselines.name: DPO
baselines.fair_comparison: For the comparison with knowledge editing, the authors use the additional SafeEdit_test_ALL dataset because traditional detoxification and knowledge-editing methods have different training and testing data settings.

baselines.name: Self-Reminder
baselines.fair_comparison: Compared with the other detoxification methods on SafeEdit_test_ALL; the paper does not specify further matching details.

metrics.name: Defense Success (DS)
metrics.caveat: Measures defense on the adversarial input being evaluated and does not establish generalization to other malicious inputs; the paper reports Defense Generalization alongside it.

controls.name: Vanilla model
controls.detail: The unedited LLaMA2-7B-Chat and Mistral-7B-v0.1 checkpoints are evaluated alongside edited models.
controls.rules_out: Provides the unedited reference for assessing changes associated with detoxification.

controls.name: wo/Tune
controls.detail: Uses the suffix system prompt for detoxification but does not tune model parameters.
controls.rules_out: Tests whether the observed effect depends on parameter tuning rather than the suffix prompt alone.

controls.name: wo/Location
controls.detail: Edits a randomly selected layer instead of locating the toxic layer.
controls.rules_out: Tests whether locating the toxic region matters compared with editing a randomly chosen layer.

controls.name: wo/Constraint
controls.detail: Removes the general-knowledge constraint from DINM.
controls.rules_out: Tests the contribution of the constraint intended to preserve responses to unrelated requests.

controls.name: wo/SyPrompt
controls.detail: Removes DINM’s suffix system prompt.
controls.rules_out: Tests the contribution of the suffix system prompt to DINM’s results.

confounds.name: The result may be specific to the edited query or attack prompt rather than general detoxification.
confounds.detail: A high defense score on the edited adversarial input could occur even if the model fails on other harmful questions or attack prompts.
confounds.ruled_out_by: Evaluate Defense Generalization on harmful questions alone, other attack prompts, other harmful questions, and combinations of other questions and attack prompts.

confounds.name: The apparent detoxification may come from the suffix prompt alone rather than editing model parameters.
confounds.detail: A prompt-only effect could produce a positive detoxification result without the proposed parameter modification being responsible.
confounds.ruled_out_by: Compare DINM with wo/Tune, which applies the suffix prompt without parameter tuning.

confounds.name: The gain may come from indiscriminate layer editing rather than locating toxic regions.
confounds.detail: If editing any layer worked similarly, the claimed importance of toxic-region localization would not be supported.
confounds.ruled_out_by: Compare DINM with wo/Location, which edits a randomly selected layer.

confounds.name: The model may appear safer because it over-refuses or loses general capability.
confounds.detail: The authors report that edited models can reject reasonable requests and that DINM can produce repetitive text; such damage could accompany a higher defense score.
confounds.ruled_out_by: Measure Fluency on responses to malicious inputs and general-task performance on TriviaQA (KQA) and XSum (CSum).

confounds.name: Detoxification may bypass toxic regions by shifting activations rather than reducing the toxicity of the regions.
confounds.detail: Either mechanism could yield safer outputs, but only reduction of toxicity in the regions would support the paper’s proposed erasure account.
confounds.ruled_out_by: Use a toxic probe to measure toxicity reduction and activation shift for the toxic regions. The authors describe the resulting mechanistic account as preliminary and hypothetical.

evidence_standards.name: DINM repeated experiments and standard deviation
evidence_standards.detail: For Table 3, DINM results are averaged over three experiments, and the table reports standard deviations. The paper does not state a statistical significance test or a numerical threshold for treating results as different.

datasets.name: ZsRE
datasets.eval_protocol: Evaluated with LLaMA-2 (7B) for knowledge editing; the paper says its model and dataset settings follow Yao et al. (2023). ZsRE is a QA dataset with equivalence neighbors generated by back-translation; the expanded version also supports portability evaluation using facts related to the edited target object. The paper does not specify a split or trial count.

datasets.name: CounterFact
datasets.eval_protocol: Uses 1,000 randomly selected facts for the single-edit experiments; also evaluates batched edits at varying batch sizes, up to 10,000 for EMMET/MEMIT comparisons. Reports the model-editing metrics described in the paper. No split is specified.

datasets.name: zsRE
datasets.eval_protocol: Evaluates EMMET and MEMIT batched editing on GPT2-XL, GPT-J, and Llama-2-7b, with batch sizes up to 10,000 and single- and multiple-layer settings. No split or additional scoring protocol is specified.

datasets.name: GLUE
datasets.eval_protocol: Downstream evaluation on Llama-2-7b for SST2, MRPC, NLI, and linguistic acceptability classification. Reports performance before editing and after five independent edits of batch size 256; the split and scoring details are not specified.

baselines.name: ROME (r-ROME in the experiments)
baselines.fair_comparison: Compared with MEMIT on the same models and CounterFact setting for single-layer editing; the paper uses the more stable r-ROME variant. No additional matched hyperparameter-selection protocol is specified.

baselines.name: MEMIT
baselines.fair_comparison: Compared with EMMET on the same models and datasets across batch sizes, using single-layer comparisons to compare the objectives directly and also comparisons with the MEMIT edit-distribution algorithm applied across layers.

metrics.name: Generation Entropy (GE)
metrics.caveat: The paper says GE drops when generated text is repetitive; it reports GE alongside the editing scores.

controls.name: Unedited model on downstream GLUE tasks
controls.detail: Figure 6 includes batch index 0 for downstream performance before editing, alongside post-edit performance.
controls.rules_out: Whether downstream performance changes are associated with editing, rather than being present before the edit.

controls.name: Single-layer editing without edit distribution
controls.detail: Compares single-layer MEMIT with its multiple-layer edit-distribution setting; the paper also compares the objectives in single-layer settings.
controls.rules_out: That differences attributed to the editing objective are instead due to distributing edits across layers.

confounds.name: MEMIT's edit-distribution algorithm, rather than its optimization objective, explains its performance
confounds.detail: A comparison that mixes the objective with the multi-layer distribution algorithm could make the algorithm appear to perform differently because of distribution rather than the objective.
confounds.ruled_out_by: Compare ROME and MEMIT in single-layer settings, and examine MEMIT with and without edit distribution; the paper reports similar single-edit performance without distribution.

confounds.name: Downstream degradation is caused by MEMIT's least-squares constraint rather than by editing more generally
confounds.detail: If the least-squares constraint caused degradation, the equality-constrained EMMET might retain downstream performance better than MEMIT.
confounds.ruled_out_by: Evaluate both methods on four GLUE tasks after batch-size-256 edits; the paper reports that both EMMET and MEMIT degrade the model similarly.

evidence_standards.name: Five independent edits for the GLUE downstream evaluation
evidence_standards.detail: For Llama-2-7b, the reported post-edit downstream performance uses five independent edits at batch size 256. The paper does not specify a statistical test, confidence interval, variance-based threshold, or other rule for deciding whether a difference is real.

datasets.name: CounterFact
datasets.eval_protocol: 3,000 samples for mask training and 1,700 held-out samples from the same 10 relations for testing. ROME uses single edits; MEMIT edits 1,000 facts simultaneously and is tested on 1,000 different edits from the test set. Reversal success is the proportion of samples where the pruned model assigns higher probability to the original object than the edited object; Top-1 Overlap is the proportion whose pruned-model top prediction matches the original model.

datasets.name: WikiText-2
datasets.eval_protocol: Perplexity is measured for the original, edited, and pruned models on a random 70,000-token subset.

metrics.name: Reversal Success Rate (RSR)
metrics.caveat: Relative preference for the original object does not guarantee exact behavioral restoration; the paper also reports Top-1 Overlap.

metrics.name: Mean probability of the target fact
MLP and attention contributions to the target-token logit (Logit Lens)

controls.name: Original unedited model
controls.detail: The paper reports the original model alongside edited and pruned models, including for WikiText-2 perplexity and comparisons of predictions and internal contributions.
controls.rules_out: Provides a reference for whether pruning restores behavior toward the original model and whether language-modeling performance is degraded.

controls.name: ROME editing without the learned mask
controls.detail: Standard ROME editing is compared with editing while the learned mask is active; reported editing success drops from 98% to 38% with the mask active.
controls.rules_out: Shows that the reduced editing success is associated with blocking the mask-targeted subspace, rather than simply measuring editing under the usual unmasked condition.

confounds.name: The mask reverses edits by broadly damaging model behavior rather than selectively restoring original facts
confounds.detail: A broad disruption could flip the preference toward the original object without identifying edit-maintaining weights.
confounds.ruled_out_by: The mask training objective penalizes KL divergence from the original model; the paper also checks Top-1 Overlap with the original model and measures perplexity on a random 70,000-token WikiText-2 subset.

confounds.name: The mask memorizes training edits or fact-specific changes rather than identifying a shared mechanism
confounds.detail: A mask that only captures training-edit-specific patterns could appear effective without generalizing across edits.
confounds.ruled_out_by: Evaluate on 1,700 held-out CounterFact samples from the same 10 relations; the paper reports reversal performance on unseen edits.

confounds.name: The masked subspace is merely associated with successful edits, which could succeed through alternative pathways
confounds.detail: If edits can route around the subspace, blocking it during editing should not substantially reduce editing success.
confounds.ruled_out_by: Inject the learned mask during editing and measure editing success; the reported rate falls from 98% to 38%, with the drop reported across relation types.

evidence_standards.name: 1,000 samples; report mean and standard error for contribution analyses, and p-values and Cohen's d for probability comparisons
evidence_standards.detail: Table 3 reports p-values from 2.9e-165 to 1.6e-68 and Cohen's d from 0.34 to 3.78. The paper does not specify the statistical test, a significance threshold, or a number of seeds.
