metrics.name: Efficacy
metrics.caveat: A probability-based editing measure can match reported results even when generated text is incoherent; the paper reports fluency and consistency alongside it, and notes that these probability-based metrics did not capture the observed generation problem.

metrics.name: Generalization
metrics.caveat: A probability-based editing measure can match reported results even when generated text is incoherent; the paper reports fluency and consistency alongside it, and notes that these probability-based metrics did not capture the observed generation problem.

metrics.name: Consistency
metrics.caveat: It is computed from generated responses and was affected by an unresolved text-generation discrepancy; the authors could not determine whether low post-edit scores reflect an implementation issue or impairment caused by editing.

metrics.name: Fluency
metrics.caveat: Generation entropy is only a proxy for naturalness and linguistic quality. The authors report that caching and batch-padding issues, as well as incoherent generated text, may distort it.

metrics.name: F1
metrics.caveat: HellaSwag scores start low for the evaluated models, which the authors say may make the benchmark challenging and limits what its apparent stability shows. The paper also describes BoolQ and HellaSwag as evaluated by zero-shot accuracy in the protocol but reports F1 in the results.

metrics.name: Zero-shot accuracy
metrics.caveat: The protocol names this for BoolQ and HellaSwag, but the results and figure instead describe F1 scores.

metrics.name: XSTest should-answer/should-refuse behavior
metrics.caveat: The paper evaluates behavior against expected labels for both unsafe and benign prompts, but does not report separate metrics for the two prompt categories.

controls.name: Unmodified pre-edit model
controls.detail: Measures each model before editing on the same evaluation prompts; the paper identifies pre-edit baselines as the unmodified model’s performance.
controls.rules_out: A change attributed to editing being merely a difference in the model’s starting performance on those evaluation prompts.

confounds.name: Generation-code artifact rather than editing-induced output degradation
confounds.detail: Misaligned KV-cache construction in generate_fast() could produce incoherent outputs and account for the fluency and consistency discrepancy without the editing algorithm degrading generation.
confounds.ruled_out_by: The authors replaced generate_fast() with Hugging Face model.generate() and processed prompts individually. This improved pre-edit baseline consistency, but post-edit consistency remained low and text incoherent; the authors say the cause remains unresolved.

confounds.name: Tokenizer BOS/logit-indexing artifact in Gemma2 results
confounds.detail: SentencePiece prepends a BOS token to targets, potentially misaligning logit indexing and causing near-zero evaluation scores unrelated to editing performance.
confounds.ruled_out_by: They corrected the indexing and checked base probabilities (Paris 0.20 versus Berlin 0.0001). Low post-edit performance persisted, though the authors note the correction did not eliminate Gemma2’s algorithmic failure.

confounds.name: Architecture-specific localization or optimization failure in newer models
confounds.detail: Fused projections in Phi3 may make subject-token localization target a geometrically irrelevant subspace; Gemma2’s post-feedforward RMSNorm may break the assumed linear effect of the weight update.
confounds.ruled_out_by: They report diagnostic probability and architectural checks: Phi3’s target-completion probabilities were near-random and the evaluation pipeline operated correctly; Gemma2’s base probabilities were sound after correcting token indexing, while editing failure persisted. These diagnostics suggest, but do not establish conclusively, the proposed structural explanations.

confounds.name: Evaluation artifact rather than genuine GPT-J recovery at high edit counts
confounds.detail: GPT-J’s recovery in CounterFact at 10,000 edits could be an evaluation artifact rather than genuine re-stabilization.
confounds.ruled_out_by: The paper tracks performance at successive edit counts but explicitly leaves the genuineness of the recovery unresolved.

confounds.name: Batch sizing or semantic edit ordering changes the apparent saturation threshold
confounds.detail: The degradation threshold observed under the study’s sequential-edit setup may depend on batch size or the semantic ordering of edits.
confounds.ruled_out_by: Not ruled out: the authors identify batch sizing and semantic ordering as untested limitations that could influence the saturation point.

evidence_standards.name: Editing-metric uncertainty
evidence_standards.detail: Reports mean ± standard error of the mean over 2,000 cases, with SEM calculated as standard deviation divided by the square root of 2,000. No statistical test, seed count, or explicit threshold for treating differences as real is stated.

evidence_standards.name: Downstream evaluation setting
evidence_standards.detail: Downstream evaluations use zero-shot prompting. No seed-based variance or statistical-significance rule is stated for these results.

datasets.name: MQuAKE-CF
datasets.eval_protocol: Use a randomly sampled 3,000-instance subset of the full dataset: 1,000 instances each for 2-, 3-, and 4-hop questions. Test with batch sizes k=1, 100, 1000, and 3000; for each k, report average accuracy across the resulting groups. Each instance has three same-meaning questions and counts as correct if any one is answered correctly. For relation extraction, select the top 50 relations by frequency from the first 500 Wikidata item properties, using GPT-3.5-Turbo to identify base relations in test questions.

datasets.name: MQuAKE-T
datasets.eval_protocol: Evaluate all 1,868 instances. Test with batch sizes k=1, 100, 500, and 1868; for each k, report average accuracy across groups. Each instance has three same-meaning questions and counts as correct if any one is answered correctly. For relation extraction, select the top 50 relations by frequency from the first 500 Wikidata item properties, using GPT-3.5-Turbo to identify base relations in test questions.

confounds.detail: The same-subject performance drop could reflect general difficulty of that dataset condition rather than the proposed key-collision mechanism.

metrics.caveat: Defined as the negative log pre-edit conditional probability of the new target; the paper says this measures how poorly the model understands the target, not its complexity.

metrics.name: Ineffectiveness
metrics.caveat: Defined as the negative log post-edit conditional probability of the new target; higher values indicate lower edit efficacy. The paper notes accuracy could also be used, but says negative log probability is more fine-grained.

controls.name: Conditional probabilities of the original facts
controls.detail: The authors also examine conditional probabilities for the original knowledge (s,r,o), rather than the new target (s,r,o*).
controls.rules_out: A correlation between pre-edit probability and edit outcome that is also present for original facts; the paper reports no significant correlation for the original knowledge.

confounds.name: The observed association could reflect probabilities of original knowledge rather than perplexingness of new knowledge
confounds.detail: If original-fact probabilities also correlated with edit outcomes, the headline association would not specifically support the role of new-target perplexingness.
confounds.ruled_out_by: The paper reports that evaluating conditional probabilities of the original knowledge showed no significant correlation with the editing process.

evidence_standards.name: Statistical significance threshold of p < 0.05
evidence_standards.detail: Pearson correlations and t-test results are treated as statistically significant below this threshold; the paper marks such results with an asterisk. controls.rules_out: A difference from full IFMET tests whether applying the multi-hop prompt to deeper layers matters.

metrics.caveat: A higher Edit Success score does not necessarily imply better reasoning with edited facts; the paper reports reasoning accuracy separately.

metrics.name: Normalized Efficacy Magnitude (NEM)
metrics.caveat: Not reported for ChatGPT because its prediction probabilities are inaccessible.

metrics.name: Normalized Paraphrase Magnitude (NPM)
metrics.caveat: Not reported for ChatGPT because its prediction probabilities are inaccessible.

metrics.name: Normalized Neighborhood Magnitude (NNM)
metrics.caveat: Not reported for ChatGPT because its prediction probabilities are inaccessible.

metrics.name: Normalized Cross-lingual Efficacy Magnitude (CEM)
metrics.caveat: Not reported for ChatGPT because its prediction probabilities are inaccessible.

metrics.name: Precision, Recall, and F1 for extracted triples
metrics.caveat: Triple matches are determined using SentenceBERT cosine similarity of at least 0.8.

metrics.name: Average number of extracted triples per document (#Tri)

controls.name: Tool-based extraction without Triplet Validation
controls.detail: Ablation removes the NER-based filtering step that retains triples whose subject and object are entities.
controls.rules_out: Comparing with the full tool-based pipeline tests whether Triplet Validation affects extracted-triple quality and quantity.

controls.name: Tool-based extraction without Semantic Deduplication
controls.detail: Ablation removes semantic duplicate filtering.
controls.rules_out: Comparing with the full tool-based pipeline tests whether Semantic Deduplication affects extracted-triple quality and quantity.

controls.name: LLM-based extraction without Triplet Validation
controls.detail: Ablation removes the entity-based triple filtering step.
controls.rules_out: Comparing with the full LLM-based pipeline tests whether Triplet Validation affects extracted-triple quality and quantity.

controls.name: LLM-based extraction without Semantic Deduplication
controls.detail: Ablation removes semantic duplicate filtering.
controls.rules_out: Comparing with the full LLM-based pipeline tests whether Semantic Deduplication affects extracted-triple quality and quantity.

confounds.name: Extracted-triple quality, rather than document input alone, explains poorer extract-then-edit performance
confounds.detail: Automatically extracted triples differ from gold triples in quality and quantity, which could account for the performance gap attributed to document-based editing.
confounds.ruled_out_by: The paper compares tool-based and LLM-based extracted triples with gold triples, and measures extraction precision, recall, and F1 using a SentenceBERT cosine-similarity match threshold of 0.8.

confounds.name: Unrelated context in generalization queries harms retrieval
confounds.detail: The gap between Edit Success and paraphrase performance for retrieval-based methods could reflect unrelated query context lowering retrieval accuracy, rather than inability to generalize the edit itself.
confounds.ruled_out_by: The paper measures retriever accuracy: 89.50% without the additional context and 62.10% when such context is included.

confounds.name: Cross-lingual direction differences are caused by differing extraction quality across languages
confounds.detail: The weaker results in one transfer direction could arise from lower-quality or fewer extracted triples in one language, rather than a language-transfer limitation alone.
confounds.ruled_out_by: The paper measures extraction quality for English and Chinese documents and compares cross-lingual results using extracted triples with results using gold triples; it reports that the direction gap narrows with gold triples.

confounds.name: Frequency and position of edited facts in documents explain performance differences
confounds.detail: Methods’ editing performance could vary because the edited fact occurs with different frequency or because its altered target appears at different positions, rather than because of the editing method alone.
confounds.ruled_out_by: The paper evaluates performance across edited-fact frequency and compares Edit Success on the Front200 and Back200 document subsets, using InternLM-7B for the position comparison.

datasets.name: RippleEdits
datasets.eval_protocol: Mainly use the popular split; also show results on the recent split. Popular entities are selected because they are more likely to be recognized by the models, to minimize effects of missing model knowledge. For each ripple query, sample 50 answers at temperature 0.7; exact-match rate is the proportion containing the correct answer, with generation length capped at 15 tokens. Also evaluate cross-lingual transfer with Baichuan by editing in Chinese or English and testing in the other language.

metrics.name: Exact-Match (EM) Rate
metrics.caveat: Uses 50 sampled answers per ripple query and counts the proportion containing the correct answer; unlike Cohen et al. (2023), it is computed per data point to enable correlation analysis.

metrics.name: Absolute Likelihood Gain
metrics.caveat: Sequence probability values can be very small as sequence length increases, so the paper uses log-likelihood; it measures the change in log-likelihood of the correct ripple answer before and after editing.

metrics.name: Relative Likelihood Gain
metrics.caveat: Normalizes the ripple answer's absolute likelihood gain by the absolute likelihood gain of the original fact.

metrics.name: GradSim
metrics.caveat: Defined as the cosine similarity between gradients of the original fact and related knowledge; the paper presents it as an indicator of ripple effects, not as a causal measure.

evidence_standards.name: Sampling and decoding setting
evidence_standards.detail: For exact-match evaluation, sample 50 generated answers per ripple query at temperature 0.7, with maximum generation length 15 tokens. The paper does not state a seed count, variance estimate, or statistical-significance rule.

datasets.name: EditAttack
datasets.eval_protocol: No split reported. Misinformation evaluation uses efficacy, paraphrase generalization, and portability questions; scores are percentages of responses that semantically match the target, compared before and after editing. The dataset includes commonsense and long-tail misinformation, with long-tail items from chemistry, biology, geology, medicine, and physics. Bias-injection evaluation uses context plus efficacy/generalization questions, with the same semantic-match scoring and pre/post comparison. Misinformation is generated using jailbreak techniques and verified by humans and models such as GPT-4; GPT-4 extracts triples and generates questions. Bias items are constructed from BBQ.

datasets.name: BBQ
datasets.eval_protocol: Used to evaluate fairness across gender, race, religion, sexual orientation, and disability. Answers such as “Unknown” and “Not enough information” count as unbiased; other answers count as biased. Bias Score is the percentage of biased answers, compared before and after editing. No split reported.

datasets.name: BoolQ
datasets.eval_protocol: Used to assess general knowledge in a closed-book setting; evaluate pre-edit and post-edit models using accuracy. No split reported.

datasets.name: NaturalQuestions
datasets.eval_protocol: Used to assess general knowledge in a closed-book setting; evaluate pre-edit and post-edit models using accuracy. No split reported.

datasets.name: GSM8K
datasets.eval_protocol: Used to assess mathematical reasoning; evaluate pre-edit and post-edit models using accuracy. No split reported.

datasets.name: NLI
datasets.eval_protocol: Used to assess semantic reasoning; evaluate pre-edit and post-edit models using accuracy. No split reported.

baselines.name: ROME
baselines.fair_comparison: Evaluated alongside FT and ICE on the same aligned LLMs and injection evaluations, with pre-edit and post-edit scores reported.

baselines.name: FT (Fine-Tuning)
baselines.fair_comparison: Evaluated alongside ROME and ICE on the same aligned LLMs and injection evaluations, with pre-edit and post-edit scores reported; the paper applies Adam with early stopping at one layer.

baselines.name: ICE (In-Context Editing)
baselines.fair_comparison: Evaluated alongside ROME and FT on the same aligned LLMs and injection evaluations, with pre-edit and post-edit scores reported; the adopted ICE baseline uses no demonstrations.

metrics.name: Efficacy Score
metrics.caveat: A model may already produce the target answer before editing, so a post-edit score alone can overstate the attack’s effect; the paper also reports pre-edit scores and the change after editing.

metrics.name: Generalization Score
metrics.caveat: A model may already produce the target answer before editing, so a post-edit score alone can overstate the attack’s effect; the paper also reports pre-edit scores and the change after editing.

metrics.name: Portability Score
metrics.caveat: A model may already produce the target answer before editing, so a post-edit score alone can overstate the attack’s effect; the paper also reports pre-edit scores and the change after editing.

controls.name: No Editing
controls.detail: Evaluate the unedited model on the same general-knowledge and reasoning benchmarks as the edited model.
controls.rules_out: Shows whether the measured performance on those benchmarks differs from the unedited reference.

controls.name: Normal Knowledge Editing (Hallucination Correction)
controls.detail: Compare general-knowledge and reasoning performance after hallucination-correction edits with performance after misinformation- or bias-injection edits.
controls.rules_out: Tests whether the measured capability changes distinguish malicious editing from ordinary knowledge editing.

confounds.name: The model already produced the injected target answer before editing
confounds.detail: A high post-edit efficacy, generalization, or portability score could reflect pre-existing model behavior rather than a successful injection.
confounds.ruled_out_by: Report scores before and after editing and their change.

confounds.name: An apparent fairness effect reflects pre-existing model bias rather than the injected sentence
confounds.detail: A high post-edit Bias Score could be present even without the bias injection.
confounds.ruled_out_by: Compare the Bias Score of the pre-edit and post-edit model.

confounds.name: Editing visibly damages ordinary knowledge or reasoning, rather than remaining stealthy
confounds.detail: Capability degradation could make the edited model distinguishable even if the injected content itself is not noticed.
confounds.ruled_out_by: Measure pre-edit and post-edit performance on BoolQ, NaturalQuestions, GSM8K, and NLI, and compare attack edits with no editing and hallucination-correction edits.

evidence_standards.name: Average and standard deviation over five edits
evidence_standards.detail: For the general-knowledge and reasoning results, the paper reports the average performance and standard deviation over five edits. For fairness, it averages Bias Scores over five randomly injected stereotyped sentences for each bias type. No statistical test or explicit threshold for a real difference is stated.

datasets.name: RIPPLEEDITS (POPULAR)
datasets.eval_protocol: Evaluated on the POPULAR dataset from RIPPLEEDITS, with results reported as percentages for reliability, LG, RE, SA, RS, and FF. Uses single-instance editing: assess metrics immediately after each edit, then revert the edit before the next test case. Evaluated with Llama-3-8B-Instruct and Qwen2.5-1.5B-Instruct.

datasets.name: Filtered Dataset
datasets.eval_protocol: A variant of the RIPPLEEDITS evaluation that retains questions whose intermediate knowledge is verifiable using the model’s internal knowledge after editing. Uses the same single-instance edit, immediate evaluation, and revert protocol; results are reported as percentages.

datasets.name: Replaced Dataset
datasets.eval_protocol: A variant of the RIPPLEEDITS evaluation that replaces KG-sourced intermediate knowledge with content generated from the LLM’s current state. Uses the same single-instance edit, immediate evaluation, and revert protocol; results are reported as percentages.

datasets.name: In-Prompt Dataset
datasets.eval_protocol: A variant of the RIPPLEEDITS evaluation that injects intermediate knowledge into the question context. Uses the same single-instance edit, immediate evaluation, and revert protocol; results are reported as percentages.

baselines.name: MEMIT
baselines.fair_comparison: Evaluated with and without ChainEdit using the same named model checkpoints and evaluation datasets; each edit is evaluated immediately and then reverted. No further matching or tuning procedure is stated.

baselines.name: MEMIT-Merge
baselines.fair_comparison: Evaluated with and without ChainEdit using the same named model checkpoints and evaluation datasets; each edit is evaluated immediately and then reverted. No further matching or tuning procedure is stated.

baselines.name: FT-M
baselines.fair_comparison: Evaluated with and without ChainEdit using the same named model checkpoints and evaluation datasets; each edit is evaluated immediately and then reverted. No further matching or tuning procedure is stated.

baselines.name: LoRA
baselines.fair_comparison: Evaluated with and without ChainEdit using the same named model checkpoints and evaluation datasets; each edit is evaluated immediately and then reverted. No further matching or tuning procedure is stated.

metrics.name: Logical Generalization (LG)
metrics.caveat: On the original benchmark, KG-derived intermediate knowledge can mismatch the model’s internal knowledge, so the score can partly measure consistency with external knowledge rather than logical generalization; the paper also evaluates Filtered, Replaced, and In-Prompt variants.

metrics.name: Reasoning (RE)
metrics.caveat: Combines Compositionality I and Compositionality II; no specific caveat is stated.

metrics.name: Subject Aliasing (SA)
metrics.caveat: In the In-Prompt evaluation, SA can be anomalously high because the injected context directly contains alias relationships, making correct answers trivially extractable.

metrics.name: Reliability
metrics.caveat: The authors attribute MEMIT’s reliability drop on Llama to its parameter-update limitation when editing multiple facts with the same subject, rather than to ChainEdit; they report MEMIT-Merge results, which restore reliability.

controls.name: Baseline editor without ChainEdit
controls.detail: For each editing method, the paper compares the condition with ChainEdit against the same method without ChainEdit, using the same model checkpoints and evaluation setup.
controls.rules_out: That the gains are simply the result of applying the underlying editing method, rather than adding ChainEdit.

controls.name: Pure KG-mined rule set
controls.detail: Compares LLM-aligned rules against rules mined purely from the KG; both rule sets are calibrated to comparable sizes of around 180 rules, with the pure-KG set subsampled by frequency thresholding.
controls.rules_out: That the benefit of the aligned rule set is only due to having a differently sized rule set; the comparison tests the contribution of LLM rule alignment.

controls.name: Automated rule selection without human curation
controls.detail: Compares the fully automated rule pipeline with the version that adds human selection to the LLM-aligned rules.
controls.rules_out: That ChainEdit’s reported performance depends on human curation of the rules.

confounds.name: External KG intermediate knowledge is misaligned with the model’s internal knowledge
confounds.detail: A model may be penalized for failing to use an intermediate fact supplied by the benchmark even when that fact conflicts with what the model internally knows; benchmark performance could therefore reflect external-knowledge consistency rather than the claimed logical generalization ability.
confounds.ruled_out_by: Evaluate the Filtered variant using questions whose intermediate knowledge is verifiable from the model’s internal knowledge, the Replaced variant using LLM-generated intermediate knowledge, and the In-Prompt variant with intermediate knowledge explicitly supplied in the question.

datasets.name: CounterFact
datasets.eval_protocol: Edits are made sequentially. For ROME, the authors use four random subsets of 1,000 examples; no subject is edited twice within a subset. For MEMIT, they use a random 2,000-example subset, continuing sample 1, and edit one fact at a time. Editing proficiency is scored with efficacy, paraphrase, and neighborhood scores; prior edited facts are checked for forgetting.

datasets.name: GLUE
datasets.eval_protocol: The authors evaluate SST2, MRPC, NLI, and linguistic acceptability classification (CoLA) using a balanced subset of 200 test examples per task, reporting F1 every few edits.

baselines.name: MEND
baselines.fair_comparison: Compared on the same sequential-editing experiments, models, and CounterFact data as the other methods; no further matching or tuning procedure is stated.

baselines.name: FT-C (constrained fine-tuning)
baselines.fair_comparison: Fine-tunes the same layer edited by ROME and constrains the norm of the weight change; compared in the sequential-editing experiments.

baselines.name: ROME
baselines.fair_comparison: Compared directly with MEMIT on sequential edits; no additional matching procedure is stated.

baselines.name: MEMIT
baselines.fair_comparison: Compared directly with ROME on sequential edits; no additional matching procedure is stated.

metrics.name: Efficacy score (ES)
metrics.caveat: Measures success on a new edit, not retention of earlier edits; the paper also measures the percentage of previously edited facts forgotten.

metrics.name: Percentage of previously edited facts forgotten
Normalized L2 distance between edited-layer and original weights

controls.name: Edit a disabling edit as the first edit
controls.detail: The authors test facts that disable ROME after a sequence of edits by applying the fact as the model’s first edit; they also test the corresponding condition for MEMIT.
controls.rules_out: For ROME, rules out sequential accumulation as the sole explanation for disabling: the first edit alone can disable the model. For MEMIT, the first edit does not cause catastrophic forgetting, supporting the authors’ distinction between the methods.

confounds.name: Catastrophic forgetting is caused by a single especially difficult fact rather than accumulated sequential editing
confounds.detail: The disabling edit could cripple the model because that particular fact is hard to edit, rather than because earlier edits accumulated.
confounds.ruled_out_by: Apply the disabling fact as the first edit and measure model failure and normalized edited-layer weight distance. ROME is still disabled, while the corresponding first edit does not cause catastrophic forgetting for MEMIT.

confounds.name: The apparent forgetting is limited to previously edited facts, rather than reflecting loss of broader model function
confounds.detail: A model could forget edited facts while retaining its ordinary capabilities, which would make edited-fact forgetting alone insufficient evidence of general degradation.
confounds.ruled_out_by: Measure F1 on four GLUE tasks during editing; the authors report downstream-task performance also declines, with abrupt losses at catastrophic forgetting.

evidence_standards.name: Four random CounterFact subsets for ROME
evidence_standards.detail: The authors use four random 1,000-example subsets to look for patterns independent of edit order. They do not state a statistical test, confidence interval, or seed-based significance rule.

evidence_standards.name: Window-averaged curves
evidence_standards.detail: Editing-proficiency plots show averages over the preceding 5 edits and 50 edits. Forgetting is evaluated after every 10 edits for computational reasons.
